reference.source: WHO Classification of Tumours of the Central Nervous System
clinicalPearls: The commonest glioma of childhood and a CNS WHO grade 1 tumour, most often arising in the cerebellum, optic pathway, hypothalamus and brainstem.
The characteristic cerebellar appearance is a cyst with an avidly enhancing mural nodule, producing signs of raised intracranial pressure and ataxia.
Optic pathway pilocytic astrocytoma is strongly associated with neurofibromatosis type 1 and may present with visual loss or proptosis.
Histology is biphasic with compact piloid areas containing Rosenthal fibres alternating with loose microcystic zones and eosinophilic granular bodies.
The vast majority are driven by activation of the MAPK pathway, most commonly a KIAA1549-BRAF fusion, with BRAF V600E mutations in a minority.
Gross total resection is often curative and may be the only treatment required for accessible cerebellar tumours.
For unresectable, progressive or NF1-associated disease, MAPK-pathway-targeted agents such as MEK inhibitors are increasingly used.
Contrast enhancement and even leptomeningeal dissemination do not imply aggressive behaviour, and malignant transformation is rare.
reference.pathophysiology: Pilocytic astrocytoma is a circumscribed, slow-growing glioma whose biology is dominated by constitutive activation of the RAS-MAPK signalling pathway. The characteristic event is a tandem duplication generating a KIAA1549-BRAF fusion gene that produces a constitutively active BRAF kinase; alternative drivers include BRAF V600E point mutations, other BRAF or RAF fusions, and, in the context of neurofibromatosis type 1, biallelic NF1 loss. Sustained MAPK signalling promotes a bland, biphasic astrocytic proliferation with piloid bipolar cells, Rosenthal fibres and eosinophilic granular bodies, together with glomeruloid vascular proliferation that accounts for the strong contrast enhancement. Despite a single dominant oncogenic pathway, the low proliferative index and tendency towards senescence explain the indolent, often self-limiting course.
additionalDifferentials: diffuse midline or paediatric-type diffuse low-grade glioma
additionalInvestigations: contrast-enhanced MRI of the brain showing cyst with enhancing mural nodule
MRI of the whole neuraxis when dissemination is suspected
surgical resection or biopsy for histological confirmation
BRAF fusion and BRAF V600E molecular testing
assessment for neurofibromatosis type 1, especially with optic pathway lesions
formal ophthalmological and visual field assessment for optic pathway tumours
endocrine evaluation for hypothalamic or chiasmatic involvement
redFlags: obstructive hydrocephalus with headache, vomiting and papilloedema
rapidly progressive visual loss in an optic pathway tumour
brainstem involvement causing cranial nerve or long-tract signs
new or worsening deficit suggesting unusual progression
reference.prognosis: The outlook is excellent, with long-term survival and frequent cure after complete resection of accessible tumours; deep-seated or unresectable lesions may follow a more protracted course but malignant transformation is uncommon.
pitfalls: interpreting strong contrast enhancement as evidence of malignancy
regarding leptomeningeal spread as inevitably aggressive
overtreating an indolent grade 1 tumour with aggressive radiotherapy in a child
missing an underlying diagnosis of neurofibromatosis type 1
confusing piloid gliosis adjacent to other lesions with true neoplasm on small biopsies
references: WHO Classification of Tumours of the Central Nervous System

management: Gross total resection is the mainstay for accessible tumours, especially cerebellar disease, and is considered essentially curative when achieved.
Incompletely resected residual tumour can be followed conservatively with serial imaging, since most remnants stay low grade and indolent.
For optic pathway gliomas, surgery is used sparingly; resection of the chiasm itself is avoided because it causes bilateral blindness, while non-chiasmatic anterior lesions may be resectable.
Obstructive hydrocephalus is managed with cerebrospinal fluid diversion (endoscopic third ventriculostomy or shunting) independent of tumour treatment.
Radiotherapy is not routinely needed after complete cerebellar resection and is reserved for multiple recurrences or residual disease where further growth would be clinically serious.

In young children with optic pathway or hypothalamic disease, chemotherapy is preferred first line and radiotherapy is deferred to avoid radiation vasculopathy and secondary malignancy, particularly in neurofibromatosis type 1.
A platinum agent combined with a vinca alkaloid is the most common first-line chemotherapy regimen for progressive or unresectable optic pathway or hypothalamic disease.
Alkylator-based chemotherapy regimens are generally avoided in NF1 patients due to second-malignancy risk.
Tumours with a BRAF fusion or BRAF V600E mutation may be candidates for MAPK-pathway-targeted agents such as MEK inhibitors or BRAF inhibitors as a first-line option in selected cases.
Routine surveillance imaging is appropriate after resection, with long-term follow-up given reports of late progression in some patients.
Optic pathway tumours require ongoing formal ophthalmology and visual field assessment, and hypothalamic or chiasmatic tumours warrant endocrine follow-up.
Patients with NF1 and an optic pathway tumour should be followed under a combined neuro-oncology and genetics surveillance plan, reflecting their more indolent course.
Any new diagnosis should be referred to a neuro-oncology multidisciplinary team for surgical planning, since extent of resection is the strongest determinant of outcome.
Urgent neurosurgical referral is warranted for raised intracranial pressure, hydrocephalus, progressive visual loss, or new focal neurological deficit.
